summary: This Standards Track document specifies a framework letting an enterprise SIP network request and receive a capability set document from a SIP service provider. The document describes the provider's characteristics so the two networks can peer more easily.

eli5.summary: A company asks a phone company "what can you do?", gets a list back, and sets up the phone link without lots of calls.

questions: what is a sip capability set document
how does an sbc get provider configuration
subtitle: How an enterprise phone network asks its SIP provider for a machine-readable list of everything it needs to connect.

tldr.problem: Connecting an enterprise SIP network to a service provider takes a lot of manual testing and hand-translating of the provider's technical recommendations into device configuration, which is error-prone.
tldr.mechanism: The enterprise edge device sends an HTTPS GET to a capability server run by the provider. The server answers with a JSON capability set document, built on a YANG data model, that describes the provider's signaling, media, transport and security characteristics.
tldr.outcome: Automation or an administrator can turn that document into configuration blocks for the enterprise network. RFC 10006 is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 10006 is a Standards Track document with Proposed Standard status, published in August 2026. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Peering Problem
sections.content:
Enterprise and service provider networks increasingly connect directly over IP using SIP. The RFC notes that "peering" and "trunking" can be used interchangeably. There are so many standards involved that it is often unclear which subsets, extensions and operating rules both sides ought to implement.

The SIPconnect technical recommendations try to fix this with a central reference, but their guidelines are not hard requirements that a peer can enforce. Interoperability problems persist, and administrators end up doing a rigorous regimen of testing, analysis and troubleshooting to find a working configuration block. Translating a provider's recommendations into configuration on several devices is another error-prone step.

This document introduces a framework for Automatic Peering and Trunking over SIP. The enterprise solicits a detailed capability set from the provider, and automation or an administrator uses it to generate configuration across one or more devices.
sections.eli5: Hooking up two phone systems is like two kids who each have a different rulebook for a game. This RFC gives one side a way to hand the other a clear, complete list of its rules.

sections.title: Reference Architecture and Terminology
sections.content:
The enterprise network consists of a SIP Private Branch Exchange (SIP-PBX), media endpoints and a Session Border Controller (SBC). The provider has a SIP signaling entity (SP-SSE), a media entity and an HTTP server that stores the capability set document, called the Cap Server. HTTPS runs between the Cap Server and the SBC; SIP and (S)RTP also meet at the SBC.

The capability set collectively describes provider characteristics for signaling, media, transport and security. Things such as the access technology used to interconnect are out of scope.

The enterprise edge element is the one that sends the request. The RFC gives two reasons: edge elements already normalize mismatches between the two networks, so they can generate configuration for several devices, and they already talk to external networks, so NAT traversal and firewall configuration are minimal.

If traffic passes through a transit provider, the capability set must account for it. For example, if the transit network does not support G.729, G.729 must not be advertised.
sections.eli5: The company's front door (the SBC) is the one who goes and asks the phone company for the list. The phone company keeps one list ready for each customer in a special office called the capability server.

sections.title: Fetching the Document over HTTP
sections.content:
The workflow uses the HTTP GET method. The server MUST set the response content type to application/json, and the document MUST be formatted in JSON. No content negotiation is specified.

The request target can be obtained by manual configuration or by discovery with WebFinger (RFC 7033) and the sip-trunking-capability link relation type from RFC 9409. The provider hosts a unique document for each enterprise network that will peer with it, so it may use credentials to decide which document to return.

For status codes, a badly formed request, such as a wrong query parameter, MUST get 400 Bad Request. A request with an invalid token MUST get 403 Forbidden. The server can use 3xx redirects and SHOULD include a Location header; the edge element SHOULD handle redirects as RFC 9110 describes.

Because the capability set is largely static, the RFC does not define a push mechanism. Edge elements poll, and polling every 24 hours is recommended. They can also use HTTP preconditions to fetch the document only if it changed.
sections.eli5: The company just asks, over a secure web connection, and the phone company hands back its list. If nothing changed since yesterday, there is no need to read it again, so the company checks once a day.

sections.title: Securing and Authenticating the Request
sections.content:
Because the information is sensitive, the enterprise edge element and the capability server MUST support TLS 1.2 or later and the https URI scheme. When HTTP/3 is used, TLS is part of QUIC. SIP or RTP over QUIC is out of scope.

Client authentication MUST use OAuth 2.0. The RFC does not mandate a specific grant type and leaves the OAuth implementation out of scope, but it walks through the authorization code grant as an example: the SBC sends the administrator to the provider's authorization endpoint, receives an authorization code, exchanges it for an access token (and optionally a refresh token), then sends the token with its GET to the capability server, which returns the capability set.

It also discusses the resource owner password credentials grant, which needs a trust relationship between the administrator and the SBC. The RFC says that relationship already exists in SIP trunking, since trunk registration uses credentials configured on the edge element, but administrators and providers should weigh the security issues of that grant type.
sections.eli5: The phone company wants to be sure it is giving its private list to the right customer. So the company's front door shows a special pass (a token) that the phone company gave out earlier.

sections.title: The Capability Set Data Model
sections.content:
The document is described by a YANG module named ietf-sip-auto-peering, a read-only (config false) model rooted at sip-auto-peering. It does not provide configuration capabilities; it is a standard format for capability exchange.

The top-level parts are:

  • variant and revision: the document version (the RFC defines variant 1.0), the time from which the parameters are valid (not-before) and the URL of a new revision.
  • transport-info: transports, registrars, realms with credentials, call control servers, DNS servers and outbound proxies. Registrar and call-control lists allow at most 3 entries.
  • call-spec: early media, forking, supported SIP methods, caller ID preferences and the Direct Inward Dial number ranges, which can be sent by value or by reference.
  • media: audio formats in order of provider preference, fax (T.38 relay and/or pass-through), RTP and RTCP behavior. Video is not exchanged at the time of writing.
  • dtmf, security (TLS versions, SRTP key management, STIR, ACME directory) and extension (SIP option tags).

Others can extend the model by importing the module and using the YANG augment statement; the RFC shows an example vendor module. The variant must change to 2.0, 3.0 and so on if a future specification defines a richer parameter set.
sections.eli5: The list has a fixed layout, like a form with boxes for where to call, which voices it understands, and what safety rules it uses. Everyone fills in the same boxes, so a computer can read it.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC includes a full JSON capability set. In it, the provider lists TCP and UDP transports, two registrars on port 5060, a realm named voip.example.com with a hashed password, and two DNS servers. It says early media is supported, forking is not, and calling numbers must be in E.164 format and carried in the From header.

On the media side, it offers PCMU and G.729 at a rate of 8000 with a ptime of 20, T.38 and pass-through for fax, symmetric RTP and RTCP, and DTMF payload number 101. For security it advertises TLS 1.2 and 1.3, SDES and DTLS-SRTP key management, and STIR compliance with certificate delegation.

The example exchange is short: the edge element sends GET /capdoc?trunkid=trunkent1456 with an Authorization: Bearer header, and the server replies 200 OK with Content-Type: application/json and the document in the body.
sections.eli5: Here is a filled-in sheet. It says things like which phone-voice formats the phone company understands and which secret-code rules to follow.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The capability set document contains sensitive information, and a leak could damage both the enterprise and the provider. The RFC calls out several attack points.

  • OAuth credentials: if resource owner credentials are stolen, an attacker could get the document and use it to make unauthorized calls while posing as a paying enterprise.
  • Transport: all communication MUST use HTTPS. Otherwise targets for trunk registration, targets for outbound calls and the credentials used to build the Authorization header travel in clear text.
  • Sensitive data nodes: the registrar, realm, call-control, outbound-proxy and number-range lists are called out for read-access control.

The enterprise cannot modify the document, so there are no particularly sensitive writable data nodes. The RFC also recommends that providers avoid hairpinned media flows, because an enterprise device left in the path can eavesdrop on the conversation between the off-net parties.
sections.eli5: The list has private details, like a key to the front door. So it travels in a locked box, and only people with the right pass can ask for it.
